title: Migration Strategies
description: Move systems safely with proven migration patterns. Learn the strangler fig, blue-green deployments, canary releases, feature flags, and rollback planning to minimize risk and downtime.

data.text: Migrations are high-risk changes that touch production systems. A failed migration can take down services, corrupt data, and damage customer trust. Senior engineers plan migrations with the same rigor they apply to system design.

The goal of any migration is to move from the old system to the new system with zero downtime and zero data loss. The strategies below help you achieve that goal incrementally, with rollback options at every step.

The strangler fig pattern, named after the fig tree that grows around and eventually replaces its host, gradually replaces parts of an old system with a new one. Instead of a big-bang rewrite, you intercept traffic to the old system and route it to new components one feature at a time.

data.caption: Strangler fig pattern: traffic gradually shifts from legacy to new services
data.definition:
flowchart LR
    U[Users] --> GATEWAY[API Gateway]
    GATEWAY -->|Feature A| LEGACY[Legacy System]
    GATEWAY -->|Feature B| NEW1[New Service 1]
    GATEWAY -->|Feature C| NEW2[New Service 2]
    GATEWAY -->|Feature D| NEW3[New Service 3]
    LEGACY -.->|Eventually retired| GATEWAY

data.text: Blue-green deployment runs two identical production environments. Blue is the current live version. Green is the new version. When green is ready, you switch the load balancer to route all traffic to green. If something goes wrong, you switch back to blue instantly.

data.title: Blue-Green Steps
items: Deploy the new version to the green environment
Run smoke tests and integration tests on green
Shift a small percentage of traffic to green for validation
Switch full traffic to green once validated
Keep blue running for a rollback window before decommissioning

data.text: A canary release rolls out a new version to a small subset of users first — like a canary in a coal mine. If the new version performs well, you gradually increase the percentage. If it fails, only a small fraction of users are affected, and you can roll back quickly.

data.title: Canary Rollout Plan
data.content: Roll out a new checkout flow in stages:
data.code:
Stage 1: 1% of users for 1 hour
Stage 2: 5% of users for 4 hours
Stage 3: 25% of users for 8 hours
Stage 4: 50% of users for 24 hours
Stage 5: 100% of users

At each stage, compare error rate and latency against the baseline.
If error rate increases by more than 0.5%, halt the rollout.

data.text: Feature flags let you turn functionality on or off without deploying code. They are essential for canary releases and dark launches. Every migration should include a documented rollback plan with a tested trigger condition and a defined owner.

items.text: Rollback plan documented with step-by-step instructions
items.hint: Include who triggers the rollback and how long each step takes

items.text: Feature flags implemented for all new behavior
items.hint: Test that flags can be toggled without a redeploy

items.text: Monitoring and alerts configured for the new system
items.hint: Set alerts on error rate, latency, and queue depth

items.text: Data migration tested with production-like data volumes
items.hint: Run the migration script on a staging copy of production data

items.text: Rollback tested at least once in staging
items.hint: Document the actual rollback time and any surprises

data.title: Critical Reminder
data.text: Never migrate data and switch traffic at the same time. Split these into separate, tested steps. Data migrations fail silently; traffic switches fail loudly. Catch data problems before they affect users.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: The strangler fig pattern replaces legacy systems incrementally without big-bang risk
Blue-green deployments enable instant rollback by keeping the old version live
Canary releases limit blast radius by exposing new code to a small audience first
Feature flags decouple deployment from release, enabling instant rollback
Always test your rollback plan before you need it
data.takeaway: Safe migrations are incremental, reversible, and tested. Plan for failure and you will rarely face it.

items.question: Which migration strategy should I choose?
items.answer: Use strangler fig for large monoliths over months. Use blue-green for complete version swaps where rollback speed matters most. Use canary for gradual validation of new features. Combine them as needed.

items.question: How do I test a rollback plan?
items.answer: Run the rollback in staging against a realistic data set. Measure how long each step takes. The rollback test should be part of your release checklist, not an afterthought.

items.question: What is a safe canary percentage to start with?
items.answer: Start with 1% to 5% of traffic. The exact percentage depends on your user base and the criticality of the change. For payment flows, start lower. For cosmetic changes, you can start higher.

data.title: Migrate a Monolithic E-Commerce Checkout
data.description: You are migrating a monolithic checkout flow to a new microservice. The monolith handles cart validation, payment processing, and order confirmation. Design a strangler fig migration plan that extracts each step safely, with traffic routing, data consistency, and rollback triggers for each phase.
data.expectedOutcome: A phased migration plan showing which features move first, the API gateway rules for each phase, data migration steps, and rollback triggers.
